title: CAN A DIVORCED CHRISTIAN REMARRY? THE WORDS OF JESUS THAT HAVE DIVIDED FAITHFUL BELIEVERS—AND THE TRUTH TOO MANY BROKEN HEARTS NEVER HEAR
paragraphs: CAN A DIVORCED CHRISTIAN REMARRY? THE WORDS OF JESUS THAT HAVE DIVIDED FAITHFUL BELIEVERS—AND THE TRUTH TOO MANY BROKEN HEARTS NEVER HEAR

Jesus spoke about divorce with unmistakable seriousness. Paul addressed abandonment. And one small Greek phrase has become the center of a centuries-old disagreement. But behind every theological argument is a human soul wondering: “Does God still have a future for me?”
There is a kind of silence that happens when someone asks a question in church and suddenly realizes everyone has an opinion about their life.
“Can I get married again?”
Five words.

But behind them might be fifteen years of marriage. Children who cried themselves to sleep. A spouse who walked away. An affair that destroyed trust. A home that became unsafe. A divorce certificate that arrived after years of desperate prayers.
Or perhaps something even more complicated.
Perhaps you were the one who sinned.

You betrayed someone. You broke your vows. You made decisions you cannot undo. And now, years later, you have genuinely repented, surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, and begun wondering whether the possibility of marriage is forever closed to you.
One Christian tells you, “God forgives. You can start again.”
Another opens the Bible and says, “Jesus called remarriage adultery.”
Both claim to love Scripture.
Both may sincerely fear misrepresenting God.
And suddenly, the question is no longer simply whether you can remarry.
It becomes something much more frightening.
“If I get this wrong, will I be disobeying the Lord I love?”
If that question has ever kept you awake at night, please stay with me.
Because we are going to examine words that cannot be ignored, exceptions that cannot be casually dismissed, and disagreements that deserve more honesty than they usually receive.
And before this is over, we need to confront something that can be even more dangerous than getting the interpretation wrong.
We need to confront what happens when people use God's holiness to crush wounded souls—or use God's grace to excuse what He calls sin.
Both errors can lead people away from Jesus.
And neither one is acceptable.
When the Pharisees approached Jesus about divorce in Matthew 19, they were not simply seeking compassionate guidance for struggling marriages.
They were testing Him.
“Is it lawful to divorce one's wife for any cause?” (Matthew 19:3, ESV).

The question emerged within a Jewish world where interpretations of Deuteronomy 24:1 differed. Some teachers understood the grounds for divorce narrowly, particularly in relation to sexual misconduct. Others permitted divorce for a much wider range of offenses.
Jesus refused to begin where they wanted Him to begin.
Instead of debating how easily a marriage could be dissolved, He took them back to why marriage existed.
“Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female...?” (Matthew 19:4, ESV).
Then He declared:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” (Matthew 19:6, ESV).
In Greek, the central command reads:
ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν, ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω.
Ho oun ho Theos synezeuxen, anthrōpos mē chōrizetō.
The meaning is clear:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Notice the force of Jesus' answer.
He did not describe marriage as merely a private agreement that could be terminated whenever two people stopped feeling fulfilled.
He pointed to God's creative design.
Marriage is a covenantal union, not a disposable arrangement.
And that matters because our culture often asks whether marriage still makes us happy before asking whether we are being faithful.
But there is another danger.
Some Christians hear Jesus' command to preserve marriage and conclude that a person must remain physically present in a dangerous household no matter what happens.
That is not what this passage says.
Jesus' defense of marriage must never become an excuse for violence, coercion, intimidation, or abuse.
A marriage covenant does not grant one spouse ownership over the other's body, conscience, or safety.
And no one should be pressured to remain in immediate danger while church leaders debate the technicalities of divorce.
Yet the seriousness of Jesus' words remains.
Marriage matters to God.
Faithfulness matters to God.
And what God joins together must never be treated as something we can casually tear apart.
Then comes the sentence that changes the entire conversation.
In Matthew 19:9, Jesus says:
“And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery.” (ESV).
Read that again.
Slowly.
Jesus explicitly condemns a particular pattern of divorce followed by remarriage.
But He also includes a phrase that has generated enormous theological disagreement.
μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ
Mē epi porneia.
Commonly translated, “except for sexual immorality.”
The word porneia refers broadly to sexual immorality. Its precise scope depends on context, and it should not simply be equated with every possible kind of marital unhappiness.
Here is where the disagreement begins.

Many Protestant interpreters understand Jesus to be identifying a genuine exception: when a spouse commits serious sexual immorality, the innocent spouse may have legitimate grounds for divorce and, in their interpretation, may also be free to remarry.
Their reasoning is that the exception modifies Jesus' condemnation of divorce and remarriage, not merely the divorce itself.
They argue that Jesus would not introduce an exception without allowing it to carry meaningful consequences.
But other faithful Christians disagree.
Some understand the exception as permitting separation or divorce in certain circumstances without necessarily granting permission for another marriage while the original spouse remains alive.
Others understand porneia more narrowly in this context, including interpretations involving unlawful unions or particular sexual violations.
These positions are not identical, and they should not be carelessly combined.

The Roman Catholic Church, for example, teaches that a valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved by divorce. A declaration of nullity is not permission to dissolve such a marriage; it is a judgment that a valid marriage bond was not established in the first place.

Eastern Orthodox churches have historically approached some tragic marital breakdowns through a different pastoral and ecclesial framework, sometimes permitting remarriage under penitential conditions.
And among Protestants, substantial disagreement remains.
Some allow remarriage following adultery or abandonment.
Others maintain that remarriage is ordinarily prohibited while a former spouse lives.
Still others recognize additional circumstances involving severe covenant-breaking, though they differ about how such conclusions are established biblically.
These are not minor disagreements.
They affect consciences, families, children, church membership, pastoral care, and the future of people who desperately want to obey Jesus.
But we must be careful.
The existence of disagreement does not mean Jesus' words are unclear about everything.
He is unmistakably opposed to treating marriage as disposable.
He is unmistakably opposed to using divorce as a convenient pathway to another relationship.
And He is unmistakably calling His followers to a higher standard of covenant faithfulness.
The disputed question is how His exception applies to the possibility of remarriage.
That distinction matters.
Because a person can acknowledge genuine interpretive disagreement without pretending every interpretation is equally persuasive.
And a person can hold a firm conviction without accusing every Christian who disagrees of deliberately rejecting Scripture.
Then Paul enters the conversation.
And the question becomes even more difficult.
In 1 Corinthians 7, Paul addresses marriages involving believers and unbelievers.
He tells a Christian spouse not to divorce an unbelieving spouse who is willing to remain in the marriage.
But then he describes a different situation.
What if the unbelieving spouse leaves?
Paul writes:
The Greek phrase is:
οὐ δεδούλωται ὁ ἀδελφὸς ἢ ἡ ἀδελφὴ
Ou dedoulōtai ho adelphos ē hē adelphē.
Literally, the brother or sister “has not been enslaved” or “is not enslaved.”
Those words are profoundly important.
Paul does not command the abandoned believer to force an unwilling spouse to stay.
He recognizes the reality of abandonment.
He speaks of peace.
But does “not enslaved” mean the abandoned Christian is also free to remarry?
That is precisely where interpreters disagree.

Some argue that release from the marriage obligation includes freedom to enter another marriage. They see abandonment as a genuine dissolution of the marital relationship and consider Paul's language sufficiently broad to include remarriage.
Others point out that Paul does not explicitly say “free to remarry” in this verse.
They also observe that the Greek verb translated “enslaved” here is different from the verb used elsewhere to describe being bound in marriage.
In 1 Corinthians 7:39, for example, Paul states that a wife is bound to her husband while he lives, but is free to marry after his death.
For interpreters who prohibit remarriage while a former spouse lives, that difference in language is significant.
For interpreters who permit remarriage after abandonment, it is not decisive.
And there is another layer.
In 1 Corinthians 7:10–11, Paul instructs a separated wife to remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband, and he tells the husband not to divorce his wife.
Some Christians regard that instruction as establishing the ordinary rule even after divorce.
Others understand Paul's later discussion of abandonment as introducing an additional circumstance that must be considered separately.
Here is the crucial point.
We must not pretend Paul explicitly answers a question he leaves open to interpretation.
He explicitly addresses separation, abandonment, reconciliation, and peace.
Whether his words authorize remarriage in the abandonment case is a conclusion interpreters draw from the passage and its relationship to the rest of Scripture.
That conclusion deserves careful examination, not confident oversimplification.
And now we arrive at the part of this conversation that may hurt.
Because perhaps you are reading this while remembering the day your spouse confessed an affair.
Perhaps you remember the trembling hands.
The messages on the phone.
The explanations that kept changing.
The horrible realization that the person you trusted had been living another life.
Or perhaps you remember the day your husband or wife simply stopped coming home.
You prayed.
You waited.
You tried counseling.
You asked God to soften a heart that seemed determined to leave.
And eventually, the marriage ended.
Now someone has told you that if you ever marry again, you will be living in adultery.
Another person has told you that God wants you to move on.
And you do not know whom to believe.
Please hear this.
Your suffering does not make every decision permissible. But neither does your divorce make you untouchable, worthless, or beyond the mercy of Christ.
Jesus did not come to build a community where wounded people must hide their stories to be treated with dignity.
He came to call sinners to repentance and to save those who cannot save themselves.
And that includes people whose marriages have collapsed.
It includes people who were betrayed.
It includes people who abandoned their vows.
It includes people whose sin contributed to the destruction of a family.
It includes people who are ashamed of what they have done.
But grace must never be confused with automatic permission.
Forgiveness and permission are not the same thing.
A Christian may be completely forgiven for past sin while still needing to ask whether a particular future action is consistent with God's Word.
That is why this subject cannot be resolved simply by saying, “God wants you happy.”
Nor can it be resolved by saying, “You are divorced, therefore your life is permanently ruined.”
Both statements fall short of the Gospel.
Consider another passage.
In Romans 7:2–3, Paul uses marriage as an illustration while explaining the relationship between believers and the law.
He describes a married woman as bound to her husband while he lives and says that if she belongs to another man while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress.
Those who oppose remarriage after divorce often appeal to this passage, along with Luke 16:18 and Mark 10:11–12.
They emphasize that Jesus' teaching in Mark and Luke contains no stated exception.
And their concern deserves to be heard.
They fear that modern Christianity has become so eager to affirm second marriages that it has softened the radical demands of Jesus.
That concern should not be mocked.

But other interpreters respond that Romans 7 is using the ordinary permanence of marriage to illustrate another theological point, not presenting a comprehensive treatment of every possible exception.
They also argue that Matthew's exception clause must be taken seriously when interpreting the parallel Gospel accounts.
Their concern is that a blanket prohibition may fail to recognize situations Jesus and Paul specifically address.
That concern should not be mocked either.
This is what responsible biblical interpretation requires.
Not selecting the verse that confirms what we already want.
Not pretending a difficult passage does not exist.
Not allowing our personal experience to become the final authority.
But reading Scripture alongside Scripture, respecting context, recognizing literary purpose, and asking what the biblical authors actually intended to communicate.
And there is one more painful reality we cannot ignore.
What about abuse?
What about a spouse who repeatedly threatens violence?
What about someone who uses Scripture to control, humiliate, isolate, or terrorize another person?
What about children who are afraid to go home?
Christians differ over whether particular patterns of severe abuse constitute grounds for divorce and whether they permit remarriage.
Some understand persistent, severe abuse as a form of covenant abandonment, even when the abusive spouse has not physically left.
Others believe Scripture permits necessary separation for protection without necessarily dissolving the marriage bond or authorizing remarriage.
Still others approach these circumstances through church discipline, civil protection, and pastoral discernment.
These differences must be acknowledged.
But the immediate duty to protect people from harm must not be delayed until every remarriage question is settled.
If you are being abused, seek safety and appropriate help from trusted people, qualified professionals, and relevant authorities.
A church should never make a person's physical safety dependent on winning a theological argument.
God's commands are not weapons for abusers.
And protecting a person from violence is not an attack on the sanctity of marriage.
Now consider something that makes this entire discussion even more personal.
What if the divorce happened before you became a Christian?
What if you were already remarried when you came to faith?
What if you and your current spouse have children together?
What if your first marriage ended decades ago?
What does repentance require now?
These are serious pastoral questions.
Christians disagree about how to apply the biblical passages to existing remarriages, especially when another family has already been established.
Some believe a remarriage entered contrary to Scripture begins in sin but should not automatically be dissolved after it has become an actual marriage.
Others believe that if a present relationship is biblically adulterous, repentance may require separation.
There are also differences concerning whether a prior marriage was valid, whether reconciliation remains possible, and how obligations to children and former spouses should be honored.
No responsible article can settle every one of those cases with a single sentence.
And no pastor should treat a complicated human history as though it were a theological puzzle without real people inside it.

If this describes your situation, seek careful counsel from spiritually mature church leaders who will open Scripture with you, listen to the facts, take your safety seriously, and explain their conclusions without manipulation.
Do not rush into another marriage merely because someone tells you that grace makes every choice acceptable.
But do not accept a lifelong sentence of shame merely because someone speaks with certainty.
The loudest voice in the room is not necessarily the voice most faithful to Scripture.
And the person who sounds the strictest is not automatically the holiest.
Jesus reserved some of His strongest rebukes for religious leaders who placed heavy burdens on others while failing to show the justice, mercy, and faithfulness that God's law required.
That does not mean biblical commands can be discarded whenever they become painful.
It means biblical truth must be handled truthfully, humbly, and with the character of Christ.
Remember the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She was accused of adultery.
Her accusers were eager to condemn her.
Jesus exposed the hypocrisy of those who stood ready to stone her.
And when they departed, He spoke words that every wounded sinner needs to understand.
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” (John 8:11, ESV).
Notice what Jesus did not do.
He did not pretend sin was harmless.
He did not redefine adultery to make everyone comfortable.
He did not tell her that repentance was unnecessary.
But neither did He treat her as though her failure had erased her humanity.
Mercy and holiness stood together in the same Savior.

We should also remember that the account of the woman caught in adultery, John 7:53–8:11, is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and is marked accordingly in many modern Bible translations. Christians differ about its textual status. Its portrayal of mercy joined to a call away from sin is consistent with teachings securely attested elsewhere in the New Testament, but we should be transparent about that manuscript question.
And that brings us to the heart of this article.
The Gospel is not the announcement that divorce does not matter.
It is not the announcement that remarriage is always permissible.
It is not the announcement that every person who remarries is necessarily living in unrepentant sin.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again, and that everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith can receive forgiveness and new life.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:11, after naming serious patterns of sin:
“And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” (ESV).
What a sentence.
“And such were some of you.”
Not because their past never happened.
Not because their actions never wounded anyone.
Not because holiness no longer mattered.
But because the saving grace of Jesus Christ was powerful enough to transform people whose lives had been marked by sin.
Maybe that is what you need to hear.
Your past is real.
The damage may be real.
The consequences may remain.
And some doors may not be open simply because you wish they were.
But your story is not beyond the reach of the Redeemer.
A divorce decree cannot erase the image of God in you.
An affair does not make repentance impossible.
A failed marriage does not place a person outside the reach of the cross.
And obedience to Christ is never wasted, even when it costs you something you deeply desire.
For one person, faithfulness may mean pursuing reconciliation where it is safe, appropriate, and genuinely possible.
For another, it may mean accepting that reconciliation cannot be forced.
For another, it may mean remaining single because of a sincere conviction about Scripture.
For another, it may mean entering a new marriage only after careful biblical examination of the grounds for divorce.
For someone already remarried, it may mean seeking wise counsel about repentance, present covenant responsibilities, and how to honor Christ faithfully now.
These are not interchangeable circumstances.
And none should be approached with a casual heart.
But here is what every one of those people needs equally.
Jesus.
Not merely a ruling.
Not merely an exception.
Not merely a church's permission.
Jesus Christ Himself.
Because marriage is not the Savior.
Singleness is not the Savior.
A second wedding is not the Savior.
Even a perfect record of marital faithfulness cannot justify a sinner before God.
Only Christ can save.
And His grace does not make obedience unnecessary.
His grace teaches us to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God brings salvation and trains us to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
That means genuine grace is never an invitation to stop caring what God commands.
It is the power that draws us back to Him.
So can a divorced Christian remarry?

The most responsible answer is that Christians agree divorce and remarriage must be governed by Scripture, but they disagree about whether—and under which circumstances—the Bible permits remarriage while a former spouse is still alive.
Many understand sexual immorality in Matthew 19:9 and abandonment in 1 Corinthians 7:15 as possible biblical grounds for remarriage.
Others believe those passages do not remove the continuing marriage bond in a way that permits remarriage.
The disagreement is real.
The consequences are serious.
And the answer in an individual case requires more than a slogan.
But the question beneath the question may be even more important.
Are you seeking God's permission to do what you already want, or are you genuinely willing to obey Him even if His answer is difficult?
That question is not only for divorced people.
It is for the married Christian who has begun entertaining an emotional affair.
It is for the spouse who is looking for an excuse to abandon a marriage because the excitement has faded.
It is for the church leader who wants a simple rule more than a truthful understanding of a complicated situation.
It is for the Christian who uses grace to justify disobedience.
And it is for the Christian who uses truth as an excuse to withhold compassion.
All of us must come before the same Lord.
All of us must surrender our preferences.
All of us need mercy.
Perhaps tonight you will close this article without having every question answered.
Perhaps you will still need to sit with your pastor.
Perhaps you will need to study Matthew 5, Matthew 19, Mark 10, Luke 16, Romans 7, and 1 Corinthians 7 more carefully.
Perhaps you will need to confess something.
Perhaps you will need to forgive someone.
Perhaps you will need to stop pursuing a relationship until you have honestly examined whether it honors Christ.
Perhaps you will need to stop condemning someone whose full story you do not know.
But whatever happens next, do not run from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Bring Him the confusion.
Bring Him the grief.
Bring Him the memories you cannot erase.
Bring Him the sin you have been defending.
Bring Him the fear that you may never be loved again.
And ask Him for something greater than the answer you were hoping to hear.
Ask Him for a heart that loves the truth.
Ask Him for courage to obey.
Ask Him for humility to recognize where sincere Christians differ.
Ask Him for the strength to walk in holiness without surrendering to despair.
And ask Him to teach His Church how to speak about broken marriages without breaking wounded people further.
Because from scandal to grace does not mean from sin to permission.
It means from sin and shame to the transforming mercy of Jesus Christ.
It means the cross is powerful enough to forgive what we cannot undo.
It means resurrection hope reaches places where human hope has died.
And it means the Author of redemption is still at work, even when the next chapter looks nothing like the one we planned.
If this article has touched a place you rarely talk about, I want to invite you into a conversation that requires courage.

You do not have to disclose private details to strangers. A few honest words are enough. And if you have experienced God's grace through a painful marital season, your testimony may encourage someone who believes their life is already over.
We want this community to be a place where difficult questions are not hidden, where repentance is not mocked, where grace is never cheapened, and where Jesus Christ remains at the center.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment available to people who may not otherwise have access to it.
But if you believe this work is worth sustaining, your partnership can make a meaningful difference.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.
You are still welcome here.
Keep reading.
Keep studying.
Keep praying.
Keep sharing the truth.
Above all, keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because someday, the deepest question will not be whether you managed to convince everyone that your marital history was acceptable.
It will be whether you knew Christ, trusted His mercy, and sought to walk faithfully in His truth.
The Savior who met sinners with both compassion and a call to repentance has not changed.
His holiness has not diminished.
His mercy has not run dry.
His cross is still sufficient.
His resurrection is still our hope.
And the broken places of your life are not hidden from His sight.
Your marriage may have ended, but the mercy of Jesus has not—and the chapter you wish you could erase does not have to be the final word over your soul.
